Key Research Thinking Patterns: Generalization and Unification: Extends results to broader mathematical classes and connects different areas through common structures (e.g., proves homological vanishing for all connected reductive groups and establishes uniform homological stability ranges across various groups and coefficients).

Structural Decomposition and Analysis: Analyzes problems by decomposing objects using their intrinsic algebraic and geometric structures, often employing inductive proofs based on rank or dimension (e.g., uses Levi decompositions and root system structures to reduce proofs about reductive groups to simpler cases).

Bridging Algebra and Topology: Translates problems between algebraic and topological settings, often using geometric structures like simplicial complexes to study algebraic invariants (e.g., relates the homology of SLn(Z) with Steinberg coefficients to the connectivity of associated simplicial complexes like the double Tits building).

Explicit Construction and Computation: Develops concrete mathematical objects, such as resolutions and maps, and utilizes computational tools to rigorously verify properties in complex situations (e.g., builds partial resolutions for Steinberg modules and uses computer calculations to verify the connectivity of specific finite simplicial complexes)
Summary Description: Peter Patzt specializes in Algebraic Topology and Homological Algebra, focusing on the homology/cohomology of groups like SLn(Z) and mapping class groups. His research centers on Steinberg modules, their connections to Tits buildings, and applications to algebraic K-theory and number theory. Patzt develops novel techniques for proving homological stability and vanishing theorems, achieving uniform stable ranges. He constructs explicit resolutions of Steinberg modules, determining the "relations among the relations." His work often involves analyzing the connectivity of newly introduced simplicial complexes (like BAAn and the double Tits building), sometimes using computer calculations, and contributes to resolving conjectures like those of Rognes and Church-Farb-Putman.
